records.title: Abwasserkanal Emscher
records.answer: The Emscher sewer moved wastewater out of the river through a deep trunk system and three pumping stations. Its phased operation is established; river recovery remains a separate, continuing task.
records.scope: One named sewer system from Dortmund-Deusen to the Emscher mouth, including its three pumping stations. The wider Emscher restoration programme, tributary projects and PHOENIX See are outside this counted identity.
records.stage: The operator records phased sewer operation from 2018 and full-system operation by the end of 2021. Subsequent river monitoring shows improvements and remaining chemical and oxygen constraints, not complete ecological recovery or independently verified AKE-only outcomes.

identity_decision.rationale: Count the named Abwasserkanal Emscher and its necessary pumps once as a defined infrastructure system. Do not count the whole regional restoration umbrella again, split its pumping stations into additional projects, or absorb the separately developed PHOENIX See lake.

timeline.event: Groundbreaking for the named sewer, as dated in the operator's 2024 retrospective.
Initial Dortmund-to-Bottrop sewer sections and the Gelsenkirchen pump entered operation.
The operator reported first functional tests at Oberhausen, including six of ten pumps.
The operator's retrospective records full-system operation by the end of 2021.

sections.heading: A sewer beneath the urban region
sections.text: The Abwasserkanal Emscher, usually shortened to AKE, is a 51-kilometre trunk route between Dortmund-Deusen and the Emscher mouth. Its total pipe length is longer because parts use parallel conduits. Deep alignment lets feeder sewers connect by gravity and accommodates crossings beneath established development. Pumping stations periodically raise the flow so the canal need not descend indefinitely. The operator's design account also distinguishes sections that can use temporary bypass equipment from deeper or higher-flow sections requiring parallel pipes. The stated century-long design life is not an observed service record. Route length, redundancy and maintenance access describe the system's engineering choices, not a measured reliability score.

sections.heading: Operation arrived in stages
sections.text: The operator's September 2024 retrospective dates the first groundbreaking to September 11, 2009. Initial sections between Dortmund and Bottrop entered operation in 2018; the final Oberhausen pumping station followed in summer 2021, enabling full-system operation by the end of that year. This sequence matters because a single opening date conceals years of partial service. The reported investment of more than one billion euros concerns the sewer and three pumping stations, not the entire regional restoration programme. Removing untreated wastewater from the river was a major change in its use. It did not make the sewer synonymous with every later ecological improvement in the catchment.

sections.heading: Testing the final pumping station
sections.text: In April 2021, the operator described a practical test at Oberhausen: treated effluent from Bottrop travelled through the new canal and was pumped onward toward Dinslaken. Six of the station's ten pumps had passed the initial functional checks. That is a bounded equipment result, not full-system acceptance. The contemporary account still treated commissioning as forthcoming, even though the canal route had been laid and earlier sections were already working. Read together with the later delivery retrospective, these records show the sequence from installed infrastructure through component testing to network operation. They should not be flattened into a claim that all ten pumps were accepted on the test-report date.

sections.heading: Making an underground service visible
sections.text: The Gelsenkirchen pumping station illustrates how necessary infrastructure can also become an accessible public landmark. The operator describes public terraces above the underground machinery and organized visits below ground. It lists eleven pumps and explains the lifting function within the three-station system. Its September 2019 completion reference is distinct from the retrospective's first-operation milestone in 2018. Those dates describe different stages rather than interchangeable opening claims. Public visibility can help explain a service that most residents never see, but a visitor description is not a current step-free-access or uptime guarantee. The capacity table contains inconsistent units, so it should not support a precise pumping-capacity comparison.

sections.heading: Sewer completion is not river recovery
sections.text: A January 2026 monitoring account reports declining nutrient and organic pollution after untreated discharges ended. It also identifies other interventions: mine-water input stopped in March 2023, and further treatment and oxygenation at Deusen followed in April 2025. The improvements cannot all be assigned to AKE alone. The same account says much of the river still lacks good chemical status, while downstream oxygen conditions in the 2024 reporting period remained problematic despite improvement. Industrial and mining legacies continue to matter. This is a more useful recovery story than a binary clean-or-dirty label: wastewater separation changes the foundation, while ecological condition depends on additional pressures and continuing management.

sections.heading: Evidence test for sustained operation
sections.text: The next account should pair sewer and pump availability with maintenance records, interruption duration and the treatment destinations of diverted flow. A repeated series needs the same asset boundary and reporting period, including wet-weather conditions that can change loading. River measurements should remain a related but separate series, with upstream and downstream locations, sampling methods and other interventions identified. This would let readers distinguish dependable wastewater conveyance from broader environmental recovery. It would also make the costs of maintaining deep, largely invisible infrastructure more legible, instead of treating construction completion as the end of the service obligation or a guarantee of every downstream benefit.

records.title: PHOENIX See
records.answer: PHOENIX See turned a former steelworks site into a lake and public landscape with flood-storage capacity. Its continuing work is water management, usable paths and the relationship between visitors and nearby residents.
records.scope: One lake and associated public-space redevelopment at the former Phoenix Ost steelworks in Dortmund-Hörde. Individual building plots, Phoenix West, the wider Emscher restoration programme and Dortmund municipality remain separate identities.
records.stage: The lake opened to the public in May 2011 and has continuing water and public-space management. The published environmental summary concerns 2021; October 2026 path renewal has a first-quarter 2027 target, not an observed completion.

identity_decision.rationale: Count the named lake redevelopment once, with its shores and flood-storage function as components. Its location beside the Emscher does not make it the main sewer project or the whole river-restoration programme. The municipal place record describes a different territorial system.

timeline.event: Steelmaking ended at Phoenix Ost, the lake's redevelopment site.
Filling of the new lake began.
The lake opened to the public after filling was completed.

sections.heading: From steelworks to public lake
sections.text: PHOENIX See occupies part of the former Phoenix Ost steelworks in Dortmund-Hörde, where steelmaking ended in 2001. Groundbreaking followed in 2005, filling began in October 2010 and public opening came in May 2011. The approximately 24-hectare lake sits within a larger redevelopment area; the two areas should not be treated as identical. The municipal history assigns delivery to the city's commissioned development structure, working with the Emschergenossenschaft, and ongoing operation to municipal drainage services. Extensive earthmoving established the new landscape. That construction history is not a parcel-by-parcel certification of remediation or evidence that every surrounding development plot has the same status.

sections.heading: Flood storage changes water management
sections.text: The Emscher runs beside the lake in a restored corridor. During extreme river flows, some water can be diverted into the lake for temporary storage; this is not continuous ordinary river supply. The city's environmental account describes phosphate removal and plant management as part of maintaining water quality. Its displayed monitoring summary concerns the 2021 water year, including nutrient input during the July flood and subsequent biological recovery. It is not a fresh 2026 water-quality result. Municipal drainage services manage the lake and nearby grounds, with the water association supporting specialist functions. Flood protection and recreation therefore share an actively managed water body, not a maintenance-free landscape.

sections.heading: Access includes more than a path
sections.text: The city's accessibility account describes multiple accessible entrances, a tactile model at Hörder Burgplatz and guidance features around the harbour promenades. It also identifies accessible toilet provision, including a seasonal south-shore facility, and adapted sailing opportunities. These are concrete ways to widen participation in the lake's public life. Listed provision is not verified availability on a particular visit. Seasonal opening, maintenance and the connection between arrival points and destinations still shape whether a trip is workable. The useful comparison is the complete journey through the public space, not a count of accessible features treated as proof that every route or activity is equally usable.

sections.heading: Renewing the walking route
sections.text: An October 8, 2026 notice describes south-shore path work with an October 7 start. About one kilometre of walking surface is to be replaced with concrete paving because the earlier surface became dusty or muddy. The work is divided into two stages, with temporary sharing of sections of the cycle path and selected bridge closures. First-quarter 2027 completion remains a target. The notice says north-shore work had already finished the previous year. Maintenance is thus part of the project's continuing service, not evidence that the original lake redevelopment failed. The temporary arrangements also show why a durable path surface and conflict-free walking and cycling require operational attention.

sections.heading: Residents and visitors share the space
sections.text: The municipal dialogue archive records discussions about noise, cleanliness, traffic and parking from December 2018 onward. Its August 2021 entry focuses on traffic behaviour near the lake and measures to manage e-scooters. Officials presented options and residents contributed observations; planned actions and completed actions were not the same category. These historical meetings show that creating a popular public destination also creates everyday management questions for neighbours. They do not demonstrate that every complaint was resolved, or establish today's meeting schedule. A durable participation process needs visible responses to concerns and a way to revisit measures after they have been used in practice.

sections.heading: Evidence test for a maintained public asset
sections.text: The next lake account should bring together dated water-quality results, flood-storage events, path-condition records and accessible-route checks. Each should identify the responsible operator and the period covered. Flood performance should describe the event and storage used, not imply protection from every possible storm. Public-space reporting should follow whether temporary diversions end as planned and whether residents' concerns lead to effective changes. These records would support a fuller account of the lake as an everyday service rather than only a redevelopment image. They would also allow comparison with other restored industrial sites without confusing land development, ecological recovery and visitor satisfaction.

records.title: Dortmund
records.answer: Dortmund's transition is visible in housing pressure, heat planning, flood mapping and park maintenance. These systems need different evidence: approved funding, modelled capacity and installed equipment are not interchangeable outcomes.
records.scope: One municipality of Dortmund. Statistical subdistricts, individual housing sites, mapped stream catchments and the wider Ruhr region are not additional counted places. AKE and PHOENIX See retain their separate project boundaries.
records.stage: Dated municipal accounts describe housing conditions, intermediate heat planning, initial flood-map coverage and installed waste equipment. Reporting years, future models and observed provision remain separate; no composite city ranking or universal service guarantee is admitted.

identity_decision.rationale: Count Dortmund once as a municipal place whose service systems can be followed over time. Its 170 statistical monitoring units are analytical subdivisions, not additional place identities. The city's role in regional water and housing networks does not extend this record to the entire Ruhr region.

timeline.event: The city reported a completed energy-use plan and intermediate heat-planning results.
Initial detailed river-flood maps were announced for the Marksbach and Heisterbach catchments.
The municipal housing summary reported conditions in 2025.
The city news article reported 92 installed sensor-equipped waste bins.

sections.heading: Housing supply and access diverge
sections.text: Dortmund's September 2026 housing summary describes the 2025 market: 898 completed homes, falling construction activity and continued pressure on lower-income households and large families. Record funding of 109.5 million euros supported approval of construction or modernization for 604 affordable homes. Funding approvals are not completed new homes. The city also describes an expected loss of rent-restricted stock as existing commitments expire. This means construction, renewal and retention must be read together. The reported decline in registered population reflects register corrections, not demonstrated relief in housing demand. A headline investment total alone cannot show whether suitable homes become available to households seeking them.

sections.heading: Looking below the city average
sections.text: The housing office describes two complementary scales of observation. Its annual city report combines official statistics with qualitative input from housing-market participants. Small-area monitoring examines 170 statistical subdistricts, using maps and indicators to identify places where housing or social conditions may require attention. That more detailed work is published on a three- to four-year cycle, not continuously. A third, regional strand recognizes that housing choices cross municipal boundaries. These different scales can explain why a stable city-wide figure masks concentrated pressure. They are analytical tools, not a current eligibility assessment for a household or evidence that every neighbourhood faces the same conditions.

sections.heading: Heat models are not connections
sections.text: The March 2026 energy notice distinguishes a completed energy-use plan from intermediate municipal heat-planning results. Its simulation suggests that heat networks could eventually serve up to 55 percent of demand; that is not a measured connected share. The model also helped select pilot neighbourhoods. The city's heat-information page explains that prospective network areas may change as planning becomes more detailed. An energy-use model is therefore useful for choosing where to investigate, not a promise of service at a particular address. The March summer-completion forecast does not establish final adoption. Legal guidance on the undated page carries an explicit updating warning and should not be treated as current individual advice.

sections.heading: Mapping different kinds of flooding
sections.text: In August 2026, municipal drainage services announced detailed river-flood maps for the Marksbach and Heisterbach catchments. These maps concern water overtopping streams, while the separate heavy-rainfall map addresses surface runoff away from watercourses. The first catchments are not full city-wide coverage. The city describes staged surveys because channel profiles, bridges and constrictions must be measured to support hydraulic simulations. Conditions can change through sediment, vegetation and flood events, making updates necessary. For readers, the important distinction is between mapped hazard, the particular scenario represented and an observed flood. A model helps target preparedness but does not certify that an individual property is safe.

sections.heading: Sensors support a collection service
sections.text: The October 9 municipal article reports 92 sensor-equipped waste bins installed in parks and the zoo. Fill-level information reaches the parks department so staff can adjust collection routes rather than relying only on fixed schedules. Larger enclosed containers and compaction also change how much waste each unit can hold. Installed equipment is not measured service improvement. Supplier claims about large potential savings are not a Dortmund operating result, and cleaner parks require collection and maintenance as well as data. The article also distinguishes completed staff training from training still planned for external providers. The useful follow-up is whether the information leads to timely, reliable work.

sections.heading: Evidence test for everyday transition
sections.text: A stronger Dortmund account would follow the same service boundaries over successive periods. Housing reporting should connect completions and expiring affordability commitments with allocations and household needs. Heat reporting should distinguish model updates, approved plans, construction and connected demand. Flood mapping needs clear coverage and revision dates, while waste services need actual collection performance and maintenance costs. These measures should be readable at neighbourhood scale without turning statistical subdivisions into competing city identities. Together they would show whether investment and planning improve daily life, while preserving the different responsibilities and time horizons of landlords, utilities, municipal departments and residents.
